metadata.title: Same Text, Better Scaffold
metadata.subtitle: Access Scaffolding vs. Text Substitution in ELA
metadata.purpose: Answer one real question in the Teardown register: when a below-level reader can't access grade-level text, is the fix an easier version, or the same text with access scaffolds around it? Explains the machinery on both sides and judges the design trade-off — a scaffold keeps the same text and eventually fades; an easier book swaps the goal out entirely.

beats.narration_text: Liam here, in for Bear. Here's what's actually happening when a teacher swaps a hard passage for an easier one — they've optimized for the reading and sacrificed the standard. Scaffold the same text instead, and you're optimizing the other way.

beats.narration_text: Look at what the scaffolded tier actually contains. The First Amendment, word for word — identical to the clean tier. What's added around it: a border, a reading protocol — circle the main idea, underline the evidence — and a two-word gloss on 'amendment' and 'ratified.' Nothing subtracted from the text. Everything added to the entry.

Under the hood the scaffold does three things: it breaks the reading into steps, it pre-teaches the two words that would stall a below-level reader, and it caps how much working memory the passage demands. What it doesn't touch is the target. Both tiers land on the same argument. They added entry structure without moving the goal.

A scaffold and a crutch look identical while they're attached — both raise performance. The design difference only shows on removal. A scaffold was engineered to fade as skill grows; a crutch does the reading in the student's place. Take it away — if comprehension collapses on removal, the support was never a scaffold. It was optimized for the wrong outcome.

production_viz.label: SCAFFOLD OR CRUTCH
production_viz.caption: does the learning hold without it?

beats.narration_text: The fade is where the design commitment shows. Once a student can read the passage with support, the scaffolds come off in an order — glossary first, sentence starters next — until the same text stands on its own. A scaffold engineered to stay forever isn't a bridge. It's a detour dressed up as one.

production_viz.label: THE FADING SCHEDULE
production_viz.caption: one scaffold removed at a time

beats.narration_text: An easier book optimizes for reading and sacrifices the standard. The same text, scaffolded and later unscaffolded, keeps both.

beats.narration_text: Your turn — in your own classroom. Pick a passage from your next lesson. Give it to Claude as scaffold-plus-passage, not as replace-and-rewrite. Then run the design test I'd run: put both versions side by side. Are the words identical? If Claude changed even one, it optimized for its own fluency at the expense of your standard. Push back and ask again.

props.command: Here is a reading passage. Generate an access-scaffolded version for below-level readers: add a reading protocol (circle main idea, underline evidence, flag unknown words), a vocabulary gloss for the two hardest words, and one comprehension anchor question. Do not change any words in the passage — the text must be identical.

beats.narration_text: Here is a prompt you can paste directly into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini. Bring a passage from your next lesson, and it will do the mechanical work — a scaffolded version with the original words untouched, and a fade schedule for taking the scaffolds back off. Then go deeper: what's the earliest behavioral signal that a scaffold has become a crutch — and how would you catch it in the next quiz, not at the end of the unit?

llm_exercise.prompt: I'm a 7th-grade ELA teacher with a class that includes below-grade-level readers. I want to build access scaffolds around grade-level text instead of substituting an easier text. Take this passage — [PASTE PASSAGE HERE] — and produce two artifacts. (1) A scaffolded version that leaves the passage's words completely unchanged but adds a border, a reading protocol (circle the main idea, underline the evidence, flag unknown words), a two-word vocabulary gloss for the hardest words, and one comprehension-anchor question. (2) A fade schedule — which scaffold I remove first, second, and last as the student demonstrates mastery, with the behavioral evidence I should see before each removal. Do not paraphrase, shorten, or simplify the passage. If a word is essential to the grade-level standard, it stays.
